note: explain (GAME_SPEC §13.6): why it happens, for the debug panel. notice (GAME_SPEC §13.4): the level of the lab's notice when the reaction starts in an item, and what it says. Balanced equations over data/species.json: one that does not balance in every element and in charge fails the build. kinetics (GAME_SPEC §7): law first_order: rate = prefactor * exp(-activation / RT) * amount of `in` * affinity factor; prefactor in 1/s, activation_kj in kJ/mol. law surface: two steps in series, 1/rate = 1/surface + 1/transport. At the surface: prefactor * exp(-activation / RT) * the area of the solid `in` (from its amount, molar volume and particle count) * the molality of the solute `driver`, if any, to the power driver_order (1 if not given) * affinity factor; prefactor in mol/m2/s. By transport: the driver, or else the reaction's dissolved species, diffusing to or from the particles (data/solutions.json's diffusion coefficients), faster as the cell is stirred. Where `in` is a product, nucleation (1/kg of solvent/s) * (S - 1)^nucleation_order new particles form per second, S the supersaturation exp(A/RT). Stirred, its crystals breed (Stage 66): secondary (1/s per W/kg of the stirring per kg of the crystals) * (S - 1)^secondary_order more, fragments chipped off them. law equilibrium: fast against the step, so each step takes it to its equilibrium in every cell (GAME_SPEC §8). A reaction without kinetics does not run on its own. Sources: docs/DATA_SOURCES.md.

reactions.explain: Heated, malachite comes apart: its carbonate leaves as carbon dioxide and its hydroxide as steam, and black copper oxide stays. The gases leaving make it run forward at any temperature, but breaking its bonds takes a lot of energy (148 kJ/mol), so it is slow until the flask is hot.

notice.says: the malachite is breaking down: carbon dioxide and steam leave it, and black copper oxide stays

reactions.explain: The acid eats the black copper oxide at its surface: its hydrogen ions take the oxide's oxygen as water, and blue copper ions go into the solution. It is limited by the reaction at that surface, not by the acid reaching it: more surface, stronger acid and above all heat speed it; stirring hardly does.

notice.says: the copper oxide dissolves in the acid: the solution turns blue

reactions.explain: Water evaporates until the gas over it holds as much steam as it can at that temperature; at 100 C that is all of it, and the water boils. It is fast against a step, so it is always at that balance.

notice.says: water evaporates, or steam condenses

reactions.explain: A solution holding more copper sulfate than it can at its temperature is supersaturated, and the salt comes out of it as blue crystals, each formula with five waters. New crystals start where it is supersaturated enough; those there grow at their surface. Cooling, or boiling water off, makes it supersaturated; warming or adding water dissolves them again.

notice.says: blue copper sulfate crystals are growing (or dissolving)

reactions.explain: A solution supersaturated in it grows pale blue crystals of the trihydrate. Above about 94 C it is the stable form under the solution; cooled, it dissolves again and the pentahydrate grows instead.

notice.says: pale blue copper sulfate crystals are growing (or dissolving)

reactions.explain: A solution supersaturated in it grows almost white crystals of the monohydrate. It is stable only where water is scarce: in a solution boiled nearly dry.

notice.says: almost white copper sulfate crystals are growing (or dissolving)

reactions.explain: A solution supersaturated in it grows white crystals of the anhydrous salt. It comes out only of a solution with almost no water left; in water it dissolves.

notice.says: white copper sulfate crystals are growing (or dissolving)

reactions.explain: Warm enough in air drier than it, the blue crystals give up two of their five waters as steam and turn pale blue: the trihydrate. Moist air, or steam over them, holds the water in; under its own solution the pentahydrate is stable up to about 94 C.

notice.says: the blue crystals are losing water and turning pale: they are too hot or too dry

reactions.explain: Hotter, the pale trihydrate gives up two more waters as steam, leaving the almost white monohydrate.

notice.says: the crystals keep losing water and are nearly white: they are too hot

reactions.explain: The last water is held tightly and leaves only well above 200 C, leaving white anhydrous copper sulfate. Water put back on the white salt turns it blue again.

notice.says: the last water is leaving the crystals: white copper sulfate is left

reactions.explain: An acid's hydrogen ions and a base's hydroxide ions meet as water, giving out heat: the solution warms. It is as fast as the two mix, so an acid and a base never stand together in one solution: the one there is less of is used up, and what is left of the other sets the pH.

notice.says: the acid and the base neutralise each other, and the solution warms

reactions.explain: Copper ions meeting hydroxide ions make copper hydroxide, which hardly dissolves at all: it comes out of the solution at once as a pale blue powder of fine grains, a precipitate, and sodium sulfate stays dissolved. The blue of the copper ions leaves the solution with it. Its solubility product, about 5e-20, is so small that a solution with base left over holds almost no copper.

notice.says: a pale blue precipitate of copper hydroxide comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: An acid dissolves copper hydroxide at once: its hydrogen ions take the hydroxide as water, and the blue copper ions go back into the solution. Without acid a copper sulfate solution gives up a trace of the hydroxide and is a little acid itself.

notice.says: the acid dissolves the copper hydroxide: the solution turns blue

reactions.explain: Copper hydroxide is less stable than copper oxide and water: it slowly gives its water up as steam and turns into black copper oxide. Steam over it holds it back. Cold it lasts years; in boiling water about half of it is gone in half an hour; heated dry above 150 C, in seconds.

notice.says: the copper hydroxide is losing its water and turning into black copper oxide

reactions.explain: Acid eats malachite at its surface: its carbonate leaves as bubbles of carbon dioxide, its hydroxide becomes water, and blue copper ions go into the solution. The reaction at the surface sets the pace: finer powder, stronger acid and heat speed it.

notice.says: the malachite fizzes in the acid: carbon dioxide leaves it, and the solution turns blue

reactions.explain: Sulfuric acid gives up its first hydrogen ion entirely, its second only partly: the hydrogen sulfate ion is a weak acid. Strong acid holds it back as hydrogen sulfate; diluted, or neutralised, it lets it go. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: hydrogen sulfate gives up its hydrogen ion, or takes it back

reactions.explain: A copper ion in water pulls on the water around it, and now and then one gives up a hydrogen ion: copper sulfate's solution is a little acid. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: copper ions give up hydrogen ions to the water

reactions.explain: Acetic acid, the acid of vinegar, is a weak acid: in water only about one molecule in a hundred gives up its hydrogen ion. A base takes the rest as it is added, so its solution resists a change of pH while both forms are there (a buffer). Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: acetic acid gives up its hydrogen ion, or takes it back

reactions.explain: Ammonia is a weak base: in water it takes a hydrogen ion from only a few of the water molecules around it, leaving hydroxide ions. An acid turns it into ammonium; a strong base turns ammonium back into ammonia, which can leave the solution as a gas (its smell). Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: ammonium gives up a hydrogen ion to the base, or ammonia takes one back

reactions.explain: Ammonia gas dissolves readily in water, and leaves it again from a solution with more of it than the air above holds: each side at its balance with the other (Henry's law). Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: ammonia dissolves into the water, or leaves it as a gas

reactions.explain: Carbon dioxide dissolves a little in water, as much as its share of the gas above allows (Henry's law): a solution with more of it than that gives it off, as bubbles where it is far over. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: carbon dioxide dissolves into the water, or leaves it as a gas

reactions.explain: Dissolved carbon dioxide is a weak acid, carbonic acid: with water it gives a hydrogen ion and a hydrogen carbonate ion. An acid added to a carbonate or a hydrogen carbonate runs this back, and the carbon dioxide made comes off as a gas. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: dissolved carbon dioxide gives up a hydrogen ion, or takes one back

reactions.explain: The hydrogen carbonate ion gives up its last hydrogen ion only to a strong base, becoming carbonate; an acid gives it back. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: hydrogen carbonate gives up its hydrogen ion to the base, or carbonate takes one back

reactions.explain: Phosphoric acid has three hydrogen ions to give and gives each less readily than the one before: the first like a moderately strong acid. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: phosphoric acid gives up its first hydrogen ion, or takes it back

reactions.explain: The dihydrogen phosphate ion gives up its second hydrogen ion near neutral pH: with its partner, hydrogen phosphate, it is the buffer of blood and of a lab's pH standard. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: dihydrogen phosphate gives up a hydrogen ion to the base, or hydrogen phosphate takes one back

reactions.explain: The hydrogen phosphate ion gives up its last hydrogen ion only to a strong base, becoming phosphate. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: hydrogen phosphate gives up its hydrogen ion to the base, or phosphate takes one back

reactions.explain: Phenolphthalein, an indicator, is a very weak acid with two hydrogen ions to give: in water and in acid it keeps both and is colourless. A strong base takes the first near pH 9; that form is colourless still. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: phenolphthalein gives up a hydrogen ion to the base, or takes one back

reactions.explain: Phenolphthalein's second hydrogen ion goes just after its first, above pH 9: the molecule opens out and turns red-pink, the colour a titration of an acid by a base ends at. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: phenolphthalein turns pink: the solution has turned basic

reactions.explain: Bromothymol blue, an indicator, is yellow in acid and blue in base, its hydrogen ion going near pH 7: green between, where both forms are there. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: bromothymol blue changes colour between yellow and blue

reactions.explain: Methyl red, an indicator, is red in acid and yellow above pH 6, giving up its hydrogen ion near pH 5. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: methyl red changes colour between red and yellow

reactions.explain: Phthalic acid has two hydrogen ions to give: the first like a moderately weak acid, near pH 3. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: phthalic acid gives up its first hydrogen ion, or takes it back

reactions.explain: The hydrogen phthalate ion, what potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) dissolves to, gives up its hydrogen ion near pH 5.4: a weak acid of exactly known amount, the standard a base's strength is measured against. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: hydrogen phthalate gives up its hydrogen ion, or takes it back

notice.says: sodium chloride dissolves, or crystallises

reactions.explain: Water colder than its freezing point would rather be ice, but ice must start somewhere: a first crystal, which forms only rarely until the water is several degrees too cold, so water supercools. Once a crystal is there it grows fast, and the heat of freezing warms the water back to its freezing point, where it stays until the cold has drawn that heat away and all of it is ice. Warmer than its freezing point, ice melts at the pace the heat reaches it. Salt lowers the freezing point: the water in a solution is less ready to leave it.

notice.says: ice is forming (or melting)

reactions.explain: An iron(III) ion pulls hard on the water around it and gives up a hydrogen ion: FeOH2+, yellow-brown, and an acid solution. Iron(III) chloride's solution is about as acid as vinegar. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: iron(III) ions give up hydrogen ions to the water

reactions.explain: An aluminium ion, small and triply charged, pulls on the water around it and gives up a hydrogen ion: its salts' solutions are acid. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: aluminium ions give up hydrogen ions to the water

reactions.explain: Ca(OH)2 hardly dissolves: where Ca ions meet hydroxide it comes out of the solution at once, a white powder (slaked lime), though some 1.7 g of it stays dissolved in a litre, limewater,, a precipitate of fine grains.

notice.says: white calcium hydroxide comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: An acid dissolves Ca(OH)2 at once: its hydrogen ions take the hydroxide as water, and the metal's ions go back into the solution.

notice.says: the acid dissolves the calcium hydroxide

reactions.explain: An acid dissolves Co(OH)2 at once: its hydrogen ions take the hydroxide as water, and the metal's ions go back into the solution.

reactions.explain: Silver ions meeting hydroxide make silver oxide, not a hydroxide: a dark brown precipitate, and water.

notice.says: a dark brown precipitate of silver oxide comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: An acid dissolves silver oxide at once, as silver ions and water.

notice.says: the acid dissolves the silver oxide

reactions.explain: Silver ions meeting chloride ions make silver chloride, which hardly dissolves (its solubility product 1.8e-10): a white, curdy precipitate, the test for a chloride. In light it greys, as silver comes out of it (not modelled).

notice.says: a white precipitate of silver chloride comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: Barium ions meeting sulfate ions make barium sulfate, which hardly dissolves (1.0e-10), not even in acid: a fine white precipitate, the test for a sulfate and the way it is weighed.

notice.says: a white precipitate of barium sulfate comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: Barium ions meeting carbonate ions make barium carbonate, a white precipitate which, unlike barium sulfate, an acid dissolves.

notice.says: a white precipitate of barium carbonate comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: An acid dissolves barium carbonate: its hydrogen ions take the carbonate as hydrogen carbonate, and then as carbon dioxide.

notice.says: the acid dissolves the barium carbonate

reactions.explain: Calcium ions meeting carbonate ions make calcium carbonate, chalk or calcite, a white precipitate: limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide this way.

notice.says: a white precipitate of calcium carbonate comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: An acid dissolves calcium carbonate, its carbonate taken as hydrogen carbonate and then as carbon dioxide, which fizzes off.

notice.says: the acid dissolves the calcium carbonate

reactions.explain: Calcium ions meeting sulfate ions make gypsum, CaSO4.2H2O, a white solid of which some 2 g dissolve in a litre: from a strong solution it comes out as fine needles.

notice.says: white gypsum comes out of the solution

reactions.explain: Ammonia binds to a copper ion through its lone pair: CuNH3 2+. With more ammonia up to four bind, and the pale blue of copper turns a deep royal blue. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: ammonia binds to copper ions

reactions.explain: Two ammonia molecules bound to one copper ion: Cu(NH3)2 2+. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: a second ammonia binds to copper

reactions.explain: Three ammonia molecules bound to one copper ion: Cu(NH3)3 2+. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: a third ammonia binds to copper

reactions.explain: Four ammonia molecules bound to one copper ion, the tetrammine Cu(NH3)4 2+: a deep royal blue, the test for copper. It also dissolves copper hydroxide that a little ammonia first brought down. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: copper's deep blue ammine forms

reactions.explain: Ammonia binds to a silver ion: AgNH3+. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: ammonia binds to silver ions

reactions.explain: Two ammonia molecules bound to a silver ion, Ag(NH3)2+: so few free silver ions are left that silver chloride dissolves in ammonia (the test that tells it from silver bromide and iodide). Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: silver's ammine forms: silver chloride dissolves in ammonia

reactions.explain: In a strong base zinc takes hydroxide ions around itself, Zn(OH)3-: zinc hydroxide, amphoteric, dissolves again in excess base. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: zinc takes hydroxide in a strong base

reactions.explain: In a stronger base still, the zincate ion Zn(OH)4 2-. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: zincate forms

reactions.explain: In a strong base aluminium takes four hydroxide ions, the aluminate Al(OH)4-: aluminium hydroxide, amphoteric, dissolves again in excess base. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: aluminate forms: aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess base

reactions.explain: Thiocyanate binds to an iron(III) ion, FeSCN 2+: a blood red so intense that a trace of iron shows (the test for iron(III)). Fast, so always at its balance: more iron or more thiocyanate deepens it, Le Chatelier's principle at work.

notice.says: iron(III) and thiocyanate make a blood red complex

reactions.explain: Two thiocyanates on one iron(III) ion, Fe(SCN)2+, deeper red still, where thiocyanate is plentiful. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: a second thiocyanate binds to iron(III)

reactions.explain: Four chlorides around a cobalt ion, tetrahedral CoCl4 2-: blue. Pink cobalt chloride turns blue in strong hydrochloric acid, or when warmed, which favours it (its formation takes in heat), and pink again when diluted or cooled. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: cobalt turns blue as chloride gathers round it

reactions.explain: Chromate takes a hydrogen ion in acid: hydrogen chromate, HCrO4-. Fast, so always at its balance.

notice.says: chromate takes a hydrogen ion

reactions.explain: In acid two chromate ions join into one dichromate ion, giving up a water: yellow chromate turns orange. A base turns it back to yellow. Fast, so always at its balance.

reactions.explain: Silver chloride dissolves in ammonia as the diammine silver ion: so few free silver ions are left that its solubility product is no longer reached. Fast, so always at its balance.

reactions.explain: Silver oxide dissolves in ammonia as the diammine silver ion. Fast, so always at its balance.
